source.title: Wide Graph Neural Networks: Aggregation Provably Leads to Exponentially Trainability Loss
source.authors: Wei Huang; Yayong Li; Wei-Tao Du; R. Xu; Jie Yin; Ling Chen; Miao Zhang

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; no cutoff or garbling materially affects the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports that very wide GCNs lose trainability as depth grows, refining the broad claim that larger networks trained by gradient methods reach low training error. Its graph node-classification setting and trainability measures do not match the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's GCN depth sweep reports training accuracy in Figure 2; its text states accuracy drops dramatically as depth grows. Figure 1 reports GNTK convergence rates, and Figure 4 compares training-loss curves with and without edge sampling. The paper does not test the listed CIFAR, two-layer ReLU, initialization, learning-rate, or batch-normalization conditions. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reports depth-dependent optimization failure in graph convolutional networks and analyzes their kernels. None of V1–V6 names this graph node-classification setting or its aggregation mechanism. The residual-kernel comparisons do not test training error in the image convolutional networks specified by V3. Activation-matched initialization is adopted without a comparative training experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors attribute asymptotic trainability loss in wide GCNs to aggregation-induced exponential GNTK collapse. Residual aggregation slows collapse, while residual MLP connections do not reduce its stated rate; neither fundamentally resolves it. They conclude that Critical DropEdge mitigates the problem empirically.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes graph convolutional networks on node classification using GNTK theory and graph benchmarks; this differs from the listed fully connected or convolutional image classification recipes. Its empirical depth sweep uses a width of 1,000 and measures accuracy, while its kernel analysis uses the infinite-width limit.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth changes training and test accuracy in the tested GCNs. Residual aggregation changes the reported GNTK convergence rate relative to vanilla and residual MLP GNTK. Critical DropEdge changes the training-loss curves relative to no edge dropping and DropEdge.

fits_no_version.finding: Width-1,000 GCNs show dramatically declining training accuracy as depth increases from 2 to 29 on Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed after 300 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide GCNs can lose trainability with increasing depth on graph node-classification tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized GNTK entries collapse exponentially with depth. Residual aggregation slows this collapse; residual MLP connections retain the stated vanilla bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual connections have placement-dependent, limited effects on depth-induced GNTK collapse.

fits_no_version.finding: Critical DropEdge yields faster training-loss convergence and lower final loss than no edge dropping or DropEdge in the reported Cora and Citeseer settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Critical DropEdge improves optimization in the tested deep GCN configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix G.3 and Figure 5 report that Critical DropEdge prevents normalized GNTK entries from converging to one common value in the illustrated experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Critical DropEdge can change the limiting kernel behavior rather than merely slow kernel collapse.

record.problems: The depth-sweep accuracy values are shown only in Figure 2, with no numerical values stated in the text. The depth sweep reports training and test accuracy, not training classification error. The GNTK convergence measurements are proxies for trainability. The reported training-loss comparisons in Figure 4 have no numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were omitted. Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5 report test accuracy for edge-sampling methods, not the training-error or trainability results required here. Cited prior-work results were excluded.

untested.parts: All parts: training classification error of sufficiently large image CNNs on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and the stated recipe qualifications.
All parts: teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima, and extra student neurons.
All parts: training-error degradation and identity-shortcut prevention in the specified image CNNs, longer training, and the tanh and Fixup exceptions.
All comparative training claims about initialization, learning speed, trainable depth, orthogonal weights, and orthogonal convolution kernels.
All parts: stability thresholds, above-threshold recovery, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
All parts: batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and the Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6 because every row is outside their scope; this does not negate the reported GCN findings. Training accuracy can express training classification error through its complement, so accuracy versus error is not itself the exclusion reason. No omitted result bears on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 classification error, random or corrupted labels, SGD/Adam comparison, model size, early stopping and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus identity-shortcut batch-normalized convolutional networks on ImageNet or CIFAR-10; special initialization for plain tanh networks; residual networks without normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Learning rates above the stability limit, loss-curvature dynamics and edge-of-stability behavior.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual networks without normalization.
